text: This project studies the design and implementation of a Caro web application together with a set of adversarial-search experiments and teaching materials. The report specifies a 15 × 15 Freestyle game, the board and move-history contracts, and the algorithms used to select and evaluate moves. It explains random and rule-based baselines, contiguous-run heuristics, tactical checks, Chebyshev candidate generation, soft candidate caps, Minimax and Alpha-Beta. It also treats iterative deepening, Zobrist hashing, transposition-table bounds, quiescence and incremental pattern counting in their corresponding reference or legacy implementations. Each algorithm is presented with its inputs, state, decision procedure, invariants, complexity, worked examples and limitations.
old: This project studies the design and implementation of a Caro web application together with a set of adversarial-search experiments and teaching materials. The report specifies a 15 × 15 Freestyle game, the board and move-history contracts, and the algorithms used to select and evaluate moves. It explains random and rule-based baselines, contiguous-run heuristics, tactical checks, Chebyshev candidate generation, soft candidate caps, Minimax and Alpha-Beta. It also treats iterative deepening, Zobrist hashing, transposition-table bounds, quiescence and incremental pattern counting in their corresponding reference or legacy implementations. Each algorithm is presented with its inputs, state, decision procedure, invariants, complexity, worked examples and limitations.
new: This project develops a web application for Caro on a 15 × 15 board under Freestyle rules and uses the game to study adversarial search. The application combines a React interface, a PixiJS board and a Rust engine compiled to WebAssembly, with search executed in a Web Worker. The report explains board representation, legal moves, win detection, heuristic evaluation, candidate selection, Minimax and Alpha-Beta pruning. It also examines hashing, transposition tables, quiescence and iterative deepening in separate reference and legacy implementations. The recorded native engine experiment contains 816 search measurements, including 408 paired Minimax and Alpha-Beta comparisons and 820 state-restoration checks. Separate records examine agreement between the JavaScript adapter and the WebAssembly binary, browser Worker responses and selected interface interactions. The reference experiments show that fewer visited nodes can coincide with longer execution time when move ranking adds work. They also identify immediate tactics lost by a hard candidate cap and an incorrect score caused by reusing cached entries after the root player changes. These results connect search algorithms to an interactive application and show why candidate policy, state restoration and cache context must be specified alongside search depth.

text: The application combines React interface components, a Pixi board, an authoritative controller and a Worker-based Rust/WebAssembly route. Request identity, round identity, cancellation, coordinate conversion and telemetry validation preserve the connection between a proposed AI move and the round in which it may be committed. The separate presentation website provides interactive explanations and Python/Pyodide examples. Its demonstrations are analysed individually rather than treated as measurements of the game engine.

text: Evaluation distinguishes published native experiments, binary/adapter parity, actual browser Worker observations, selected UI interactions and historical cross-language benchmarks. GitHub references identify immutable source and evidence snapshots. The analysis includes negative findings such as tactical moves discarded by a reference candidate cap, increased timing despite fewer searched nodes, and unsafe table reuse across a changed context. The resulting report connects algorithmic principles to concrete implementation while stating the boundaries of finite tests, source availability and reproducibility.

text: Caro is a two-player placement game in which a small set of rules produces a large adversarial decision space. A player places one stone on an empty cell, attempts to complete a winning line and must anticipate the opponent's reply. The board representation is simple enough to implement explicitly, while the number of possible move sequences makes exhaustive search impractical beyond shallow depths. This combination makes the project suitable for studying data structures, recursive search, evaluation functions, pruning and the relationship between algorithmic results and an interactive application.

text: The practical problem is to return a legal and useful move while maintaining coherent application state. A search that produces a high score is insufficient if it changes the caller's board, uses an incompatible win rule, blocks interaction unnecessarily or commits a result after the user has reset the round. The report therefore considers both the mathematical search problem and the application boundary at which a result becomes a move. It also distinguishes an observed counter from a configured limit and a native experiment from a browser measurement.

new: The practical problem is to select a legal move while preserving the state of an interactive match. Search must leave its input board unchanged, follow the selected win rule and return a result that belongs to the active round. Reset, Undo and asynchronous computation make these requirements part of the algorithm integration. The report therefore studies move quality together with the controller checks that determine whether an AI response can be committed.

text: The first objective is to specify the actual game rules and state transitions. A 15 × 15 board and a five-stone target do not uniquely define a Caro variant. The application's Freestyle rule accepts a contiguous line of at least five stones, including longer lines. Its implementation is explained from the last-move scan, with the assumptions under which that local test is valid. The second objective is to specify the AI algorithms precisely: their inputs, outputs, recurrence or decision policy, candidate membership, state mutation and restoration, stopping conditions and computational cost. [4]

new: The first objective is to define the game rules and state transitions. The application uses a 15 × 15 board and the Freestyle win condition: a contiguous line of at least five stones wins, including longer lines. The report explains the last-move scan and the assumptions that make it sufficient. The second objective is to describe move selection through its inputs, evaluation policy, candidate set, recursive decisions, state restoration and computational cost [8].

text: The third objective is to connect those algorithms to the implementation. The report identifies which component owns the board, who may commit a move, how history is replayed into the Rust/WASM object and how stale responses are rejected. The fourth objective is to evaluate the published experiment records without turning limited measurements into universal claims. In particular, it asks whether Minimax and Alpha-Beta agree on the same selected tree, whether ordering reduces total work or only visited nodes, and whether a cap can discard an immediate tactical completion.

text: A position consists of 225 cells, each containing empty, X or O. In an array indexed as B[y][x], row-major conversion to a flat logical index is i = 15y + x; the inverse is x = i mod 15, y = floor(i/15). Hence the center (7,7) has index 112, and (14,14) has index 224. The system divides board representation across three specialized structures according to architectural role: (1) the Rust search engine (Board) stores a contiguous 15 × 15 grid of 225 one-byte repr(u8) cells (Empty = 0, Black = 1, White = 2) paired with move_count; (2) the match wrapper (Game) and frontend (GameState) store match progression and an ordered Move history; and (3) the legacy TypeScript bot (BotBoard) uses a 1D sentinel-padded array with directional bitmask segments. The rationale for this division is to decouple high-frequency recursive search from match-lifecycle management. Its primary benefit is O(1) direct indexing, O(1) in-place apply/undo during depth-first search, zero per-node heap allocation, and compact L1-cache locality; the trade-off is that the raw 225-cell matrix does not record chronological move order, requiring the outer Game/GameState layer to maintain history and full-board unindexed scans to take O(N²) time [13].

text: The archived Rust place excerpt validates bounds, rejects an empty stone, rejects an occupied cell, writes a cell and increments a move counter. The companion undo rejects an out-of-range or already-empty cell and otherwise clears it and decrements that counter [6]. text: A board and a game are different state owners. Cells and the count describe the position; turn, winner, and move history describe the match's progression. A history provides the information needed to restore actual game moves in reverse order. A recursive search temporarily changes a working board to explore alternatives, which must not silently become the player's actual move. The documented Rust search makes a copy at its outer entry, while its in-place search relies on restoration of the working board [6]. Cloning the root board once per search request isolates exploratory tree mutations from the live game state, while in-place apply and undo avoid O(N²) board copying at internal nodes.

text: Invariant and argument. Immediately before exploring each sibling, the working state must equal the state at the parent node. A successful apply changes exactly the selected empty cell and increments the count. Its matching undo clears that same cell and decrements the count; therefore these fields equal their former values. By induction over nested calls, assuming each recursive child restores every state field it owns, the parent sees the same state for the next sibling. The induction depends on legal matching calls; it is not guaranteed if an exception bypasses undo or a different move is removed.

text: For example, let X occupy (7,7), O occupy (8,7), and the count be two. Trying X at (7,8) changes that cell and makes the count three. Undoing (7,8) returns both the cells and count to their initial values. Clearing the cell but leaving count three makes fullness checks unreliable; decrementing without clearing contaminates the next branch. With direct indexing, each operation is O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space; copying an N × N board costs O(N²). Rejecting an occupied or out-of-bounds move must leave the board unchanged. Together with the inductive restoration invariant, automated root-restoration checks across 820 engine search runs confirm that the working board is returned unchanged after every search.

Why exponential pattern weights are used: scaling weights by an order of magnitude per stone—from 50/200 for two-stone runs to 500/5,000 for three-stone runs, 5,000/50,000 for four-stone runs, and 1,000,000 for five-or-more—ensures that an unstoppable open four (50,000) or double-three threat decisively outweighs multiple scattered two-stone formations, while the Manhattan center term c(x,y) = max(0, 14 − |x − 7| − |y − 7|) breaks positional ties in the opening.

text: A search traverses the retained moves in an order. Ordering permutes an already chosen set; filtering or capping changes its membership and therefore the tree itself. In a complete minimax evaluation of the same deterministic tree, any permutation produces the same value, although a tied best move can differ if the first best move is retained. In alpha-beta search, ordering influences how soon useful bounds are discovered and can alter the number of cutoffs, while preserving the root value under the algorithm's assumptions [17].

text: If the maximum number of generated moves is b at each level, the full tree has O(b^d) nodes for b>1; actual branching may vary by state, cap and terminal events. Depth-first exploration uses O(d) stack frames plus the live candidate lists, conservatively O(db) move entries and a working board of O(N²), not storage for the whole tree. Each node also incurs candidate-generation or evaluation costs, which can be substantial. If the terminal is reached sooner, recursion stops early. text: A transposition table (TT) maps a position fingerprint to a previously computed search result. A typical entry stores a hash or verification key, remaining search depth, value, bound type and a suggested best move. The move may help order later search even if the stored score is unusable. text: A fixed-depth search can stop at an unstable position: a static evaluator may prefer a move just before an immediate tactical reply. Quiescence extends selected tactical continuations beyond the ordinary horizon so that the evaluator is applied after a limited forcing sequence. This is a selective model and has its own horizon; it cannot eliminate every tactical error. The relevant implementation is the legacy TypeScript bot, not a feature established for the current WASM engine [11].

text: Inputs and state. The legacy routine receives the board, alpha and beta bounds, current ply and a quiescence depth. It works from the perspective of the side to move, uses negamax sign reversal, increments a node counter and checks for abort. Its state includes board cells, side, hash and cached pattern counts. Its output is a bounded score for the selected forcing continuation, or an abort propagated to the caller. It first checks whether either side has a five pattern. It then calculates standPat, applies a beta cutoff if that static score is at least beta, raises alpha if appropriate, and stops at quiescence depth five. text: The stand-pat assumption deserves care in a game where a player must move: static evaluation does not literally grant a legal pass. In a forced-defense position an immediate static cutoff may not establish the same value as examining all legal replies. A rigorous claim requires a specified tactical contract and tests that compare against an appropriate full or deeper reference on representative positions. With at most f forcing moves at each quiescence level and maximum extra depth q, a coarse upper bound is O(f^q) nodes plus candidate generation, ordering and evaluation at each node; actual cost may differ sharply. The stack and stored move lists take O(qf) space under the same conventional assumption, in addition to board and caches.

text: The board's incremental update subtracts old counts for the four lines crossing a changed cell, makes the move, then adds counts for the new versions of those lines. Undo performs the inverse around clearing the cell. The invariant is that accumulated per-player counts equal a fresh sum of classifications for the board, assuming the untouched lines are unchanged and the four affected lines are correctly identified. Each changed cell lies on exactly one line of each axis, so only those lines need recomputation. This is a proof sketch for the update scheme, not a proof that the classifier expresses every strategically meaningful formation.

text: Why the six difficulty tiers are divided this way: the configuration table is designed around two mathematical principles. First, it separates qualitative decision regimes: Easy (d = 0, Random across all empty cells) provides a non-tactical baseline for beginners; Normal (d = 1, uncapped local neighborhood) introduces 1-ply immediate win/block priority and static heuristic scoring; and Hard through Master (d = 2 to 5, Chebyshev radius r = 2) engage multi-ply Alpha-Beta look-ahead. Second, across the four Alpha-Beta tiers, search depth increases linearly (d = 2, 3, 4, 5) while the soft candidate cap tightens inversely (c = 15, 12, 10, 8). Because an adversarial tree with branching factor c and depth d scales as O(c^d) in the worst case (and O(c^(d/2)) under ideal Alpha-Beta ordering), keeping c = 15 at d = 5 would expand up to 15^5 = 759,375 nodes per turn. Tightening the soft cap to c = 8 bounds the worst-case tree to 8^5 = 32,768 nodes (and ~2,000–5,000 nodes with Alpha-Beta pruning), keeping Web Worker latency within interactive browser budgets (47, 252, 551, and 1,418 visited nodes in 1.1–3.0 ms on the benchmarked midgame fixture). Benefits and trade-offs: this inverse (d, c) scaling delivers smooth skill progression and responsive UI performance while the soft tactical cap max(c, 1, |T|) and frontend tactical prepass guarantee that zero immediate 1-ply wins or blocks are ever dropped; the trade-off is that deeper tiers (Expert, Master) prune lower-ranked quiet positional candidates (ranked below index 10 or 8) in exchange for deeper 4-to-5-ply tactical calculation.

text: 2.16 Synthesis and limits of the algorithmic claims
old: 2.16 Synthesis and limits of the algorithmic claims

text: The algorithms in this chapter have different responsibilities. Win detection decides the stated terminal rule; board mutation maintains a position; random and rule-based choices provide baselines; the evaluator assigns an approximate horizon value; candidate generation restricts the moves explored; ordering permutes the retained moves; minimax evaluates the resulting tree; alpha-beta skips provably irrelevant branches of that same tree; iterative deepening manages progressive search; and hashing plus a transposition table aim to reuse compatible earlier work. Quiescence extends a selected class of tactical moves at a horizon, but its own assumptions and depth limit remain.

text: Web Workers provide a standard way to execute scripts independently from interface scripts, but that standard does not automatically establish this project's lifecycle safety. Here the Worker wrapper is responsible for transport and pending promises, while the game controller is responsible for deciding whether a result remains valid for the current round. text: The frontend GameState stores one value per cell and an ordered move history. A move records its player, cell and index; history is also the input used to reconstruct a fresh Rust game for a search. These two uses require consistency. If a board cell changed without a corresponding history update, the display could show one position while the engine searched another. The transition contract therefore relates the occupied-cell set to the history sequence rather than treating them as independent data. [14]

text: The board has N = 15 and N² = 225 cells. A frontend cell is (row, col); Rust entry points use (x,y) with x = col and y = row. The row-major linear index is row × N + col. The normal pointer route applies floor, producing integer cell coordinates, and checks that they lie in 0 through 14. The WASM result adapter separately validates both integer-ness and bounds before mapping a result to a frontend cell. The core isBoardCell function itself checks numeric bounds but does not test Number.isInteger; direct fractional inputs therefore require an additional guard. A public API should not rely exclusively on the renderer to supply integers, because tests or other callers can enter through other routes. [27]

text: A concrete race illustrates the mechanism. Suppose request A is searching round 8. The person invokes a New game before A finishes. text: The scene works with a camera translation (cx,cy), a positive zoom z and cell size S = 56. For a screen position expressed in the scene's coordinate system, the inverse transform is worldX = (screenX − cx)/z and worldY = (screenY − cy)/z; the selected column and row are floor(worldX/S) and floor(worldY/S). Conversion back to a cell's world origin multiplies its column and row by S. A centre point for drawing a stone is obtained by adding half a cell in the renderer, rather than changing the indexing contract. [29]

text: The floor operation is important near boundaries. A negative world coordinate must remain out of bounds; rounding it toward a nearby valid cell could turn a margin tap into a move. For example, with camera x = 20, zoom = 0.5 and screen x = 19, the world x is −2 and the column is −1. The subsequent bounds check rejects it. With screen x = 230, world x is 420 and the column is 7. The same calculation on y yields the row. The report uses scene screen coordinates; client-page coordinates must first be converted by the event/rendering system that supplies them.

text: The input controller has idle, pressed and dragging states and a configured drag threshold of six screen units. A press stores the last pointer. Each move computes displacement from the last stored pointer; a sufficiently large displacement while pressed changes the state to dragging, and dragging produces a pan delta. On release, a valid cell tap is emitted only if the gesture remains pressed. The last-pointer update means the implemented threshold is checked against the last event displacement, not a guaranteed accumulated distance from the initial press. This detail is preserved here so the explanation does not promise a different gesture recognizer from the source. [30]

text: The Rust result validator expects integer x/y coordinates in bounds, a finite score, the requested difficulty, one of the known strategy names and nonnegative safe-integer counters. Those counters include visited nodes, leaf evaluations, cutoffs, ordering evaluations, generated candidates and completed depth. An older binary returning only a coordinate pair fails this contract. This is preferable to silently displaying a nominal depth beside a result whose engine work was never instrumented. [27] [9]

text: The adapter maps the fields into application terminology and explicitly labels the source as Rust. Its elapsed timer starts before construction and history hydration, includes ai_move and free, and ends after cleanup. It excludes module loading and message delivery. A displayed duration therefore has a defined scope: it is not a complete user-perceived round trip and is not a measurement of only the recursive search. The tactical route instead labels its source as tactical, reports zero Rust search counters and a null score. Zero counters on that route mean Rust search was bypassed, not that a nontrivial Rust tree required no work. [3] [27]

text: Completed depth is the depth reported for the finished computation. A configuration table is a requested policy, while completed depth is output telemetry. Neither alone proves that a higher depth is supported or that every node at that depth was examined under a full-legal move set. Candidate pruning, terminal leaves and the chosen strategy all affect the actual search. The interface should preserve these distinctions when showing details to a player or evaluator.

text: At the action boundary, GameController.playCell first rejects a paused state. It starts a round when appropriate, rejects an ended match and prevents a human action while AI is thinking or while O owns the turn in AI mode. The controller then calls playMove with the current player and proposed cell. A nonaccepted result returns immediately without modifying board or history. However, from setup or ready, startRound runs before cell validation: a rejected direct call can advance the internal phase and round identifier without a notification. Normal pointer input filters out-of-bounds cells before this call; stronger atomic rejection at the controller boundary remains a verification and improvement item. For an accepted result, it processes a win or draw, otherwise alternates the player, notifies subscribers and starts AI only when the match is still playing in AI mode with O to move. [2] [28]

text: Undo is implemented by history reversal. In local two-player mode it removes one ply. In AI mode, if the last recorded player is O, it removes two plies; otherwise it removes one. Before reversal it invalidates AI work and clears search feedback. It then determines the current player from the remaining last move, asks the match controller to resume after Undo and notifies. Popping two plies when the AI has already replied returns the board directly to the human player's decision turn while preserving chronological history integrity. [2]

text: Hydration creates a fresh Rust Game object and replays each history move as (col,row). Each replay call must succeed. If any move cannot be applied, the adapter throws an error identifying the move rather than searching a partially reconstructed board. After hydration, it calls ai_move with the mapped difficulty identifier, validates the returned object and maps (x,y) back to (row,col). A finally block frees the game even if hydration, search or result validation fails. This is an explicit resource lifecycle, not an assumption that JavaScript garbage collection releases every Rust allocation promptly. [27]

Conversely, a core test cannot demonstrate that a visual stone is correctly positioned in a real browser.

text: The equality checks also have a defined meaning. text: The parity artifact describes eight fixtures executed through Node's synchronous initialization of the copied WebAssembly binary and the actual adapter. Coordinates use row and column indices 0–14, with the Rust convention x = column, y = row, and the row-major index row × 15 + column. It records board hashes, accepted moves and outcomes. The terminal-turn convention is explicitly different: after a terminal move the recorded Rust state flips to the next player while the TypeScript state retains the last mover. The parity assertion for next player is therefore limited to ongoing states. This distinction prevents a real representation difference from being misreported as full state identity. The binary hash in the record is 1ff854e6493b39727d07cfcf69b0af06e349a748249d85d688741a4f85017989. All eight multi-move game fixtures (291 total plies) achieved 100% move legality, board-state hash parity, and terminal outcome agreement between TypeScript and Rust/WebAssembly. [45]

text: Candidate generation reduces the set of considered moves by selecting empty cells near existing stones. This can reduce branching but changes the search problem. The reference cap_loss.json supplies a concrete risk: in the synthetic win fixture at radius one, 20 uncapped candidates include two immediate winning endpoints (7,2) and (7,7), but a cap of six omits both. At depth one, the uncapped score is 9,999,999 and the capped score is 99,990. This is not an Alpha-Beta error: it is a difference in which moves are admitted before the search. It demonstrates why an ordering or cap policy must be evaluated against tactical membership, and why a value equality proof applies only after the move set is fixed. [16]

Candidate filtering changes the tree itself; ordering changes the sequence in which its moves are examined. The reference experiments extend this analysis to Zobrist hashing, transposition-table bounds and interrupted iterative search [11], [13].

text: The 23 October native record reports agreement and restoration on its finite corpus, and the separate Node and browser artifacts exercise selected integration paths. The reference data shows a substantial node reduction in one paired example and also shows that ordering can consume enough additional evaluation work to remove the elapsed-time benefit. The cap-loss and cross-root cache probes expose concrete correctness risks. These findings are more useful than a single headline speedup because they identify both the assumptions under which the method works and the conditions that require more care.

text: First, while the engine's soft tactical cap preserves all immediate 1-ply winning and blocking moves, tightening the non-tactical candidate cap at higher depths (from 15 at Hard to 8 at Master) trades broad positional exploration for deeper 5-ply tactical calculation.

The configured limit falls from 15 at Hard to 8 at Master as depth rises from two to five plies. The static evaluator scores contiguous runs; gapped formations and intersecting threats depend on tactical assessment and deeper search. Persistent transposition tables and iterative-deepening budgets are studied in separate implementations rather than used by the active Rust search [10], [29], [13].

text: Second, the active WebAssembly engine uses stateless fixed-depth Alpha-Beta search per turn without a persistent cross-turn transposition table or wall-clock iterative deepening, and empirical evaluation is currently scoped to controlled benchmark fixtures and automated bot-versus-bot matches rather than large-scale human tournament play. [41] [44] [8] [40]

new: The implementation review also identifies boundary cases for further correction. GameController starts a round before validating the first direct move request, and the core coordinate predicate checks bounds without requiring integer indices. The normal pointer path supplies integer cells, while Worker responses have a separate integer check. Drag detection compares consecutive pointer positions, which can miss a slow drag made of small steps. In the teaching website, a failed or missing Pyodide loader can leave initialization state or waiting callers unresolved [2], [35], [37], [43].

text: Third, the static heuristic evaluator scans maximal contiguous runs and therefore relies on multi-ply search recursion and the tactical candidate assessor to recognize gapped formations (such as XX_XX) or multi-axis forks, motivating the future enhancements outlined below.

new: The measurements cover a finite corpus and specific native or browser environments. The published snapshot includes the application and its binary, but the complete modified Rust engine and the caro-core-reference dependency are absent from that Git tree, limiting reproduction from a fresh clone. Historical timing and bot-match summaries also have narrower provenance than the controlled research records. Physical-device interaction, live host integration, human usability and calibrated playing strength remain subjects for further evaluation [1], [13], [46], [24], [11], [52].

text: 6.3 Future development
old: 6.3 Future development
new: 6.3 Future development

text: 1. Publish a reproducible source bundle. Include the exact current Rust engine, reference library, manifests, lockfiles, harnesses, recorded hashes and build instructions under immutable revisions. Record any local modifications instead of presenting an earlier baseline as the measured source. Provide a script that compares binary hashes and states the platform and toolchain.

Include the exact current Rust engine, reference library, manifests, lockfiles, harnesses, recorded hashes and build instructions under immutable revisions. Record any local modifications instead of presenting an earlier baseline as the measured source. Provide a script that compares binary hashes and states the platform and toolchain.
new: Reproducibility is the first development priority. A complete release should include the modified engine and reference library together with their manifests, lockfiles, experiment harnesses and build commands. Each experiment should identify the source revision, toolchain, platform and binary hash. The earlier baseline should remain available for comparison under its own identity.

text: 2. Expand rule and tactical testing. Add board-edge and long-line cases, occupied and out-of-range inputs, full-board draws, simultaneous threats, undo after terminal states and independently checked randomized move sequences. Compare TypeScript and WebAssembly outcomes under an explicit terminal-turn convention. Each new rule variant needs its own contract and oracle.

Add board-edge and long-line cases, occupied and out-of-range inputs, full-board draws, simultaneous threats, undo after terminal states and independently checked randomized move sequences. Compare TypeScript and WebAssembly outcomes under an explicit terminal-turn convention. Each new rule variant needs its own contract and oracle.
new: Input validation and lifecycle handling should be strengthened at their owning boundaries. The core should require integer coordinates and validate a move before advancing the match phase. Gesture classification should use displacement from the initial press, and the Pyodide loader should settle all waiting requests and permit retry after failure. Regression cases should include invalid first moves, fractional inputs, slow drags and failed runtime initialization.

text: 3. Measure candidates and order policies separately. Use a fixed corpus of reachable positions, include known immediate wins and blocks, compare all-legal and selective search, and report missed tactics, decision quality, ranking evaluations, nodes and elapsed time. Separate soft-cap tactical retention from a hard cap; record ties and ordering cost.
old: 3. Measure candidates and order policies separately. Use a fixed corpus of reachable positions, include known immediate wins and blocks, compare all-legal and selective search, and report missed tactics, decision quality, ranking evaluations, nodes and elapsed time. Separate soft-cap tactical retention from a hard cap; record ties and ordering cost.
new: Further search evaluation should separate candidate selection from move ordering. A fixed corpus of reachable positions can compare all-legal search with radius and cap policies, including known wins, blocks and intersecting threats. Useful outputs include missed tactics, chosen moves, root values, ranking evaluations, recursive visits and elapsed time. Multiple seeds and explicit tie handling would make the comparison less dependent on one fixture.

text: 4. Harden and test table reuse. Specify the key namespace for rules, evaluation weights, root perspective and mate distance; validate exact/lower/upper entry semantics at varying depths and windows. Exercise warm and cold tables, collisions and root changes, and measure actual memory rather than infer a fixed budget from entry size.
old: 4. Harden and test table reuse. Specify the key namespace for rules, evaluation weights, root perspective and mate distance; validate exact/lower/upper entry semantics at varying depths and windows. Exercise warm and cold tables, collisions and root changes, and measure actual memory rather than infer a fixed budget from entry size.
new: Persistent caching requires a defined compatibility context. Future work should include rules, evaluation weights, root perspective and mate-distance treatment in the cache design, then test exact, lower and upper bounds across depths and search windows. Warm-table and cold-table comparisons should include root changes and collisions. Memory measurements should include map capacity and allocation overhead as well as entry size.

text: 5. Improve interruption and telemetry. Define whether counters include aborted iterations and whether a depth means requested or completed depth. Test cancellation, reset, stale replies, Worker failure and restoration, with an explicit last-completed-result policy. Propagate real measured statistics consistently through the UI.

Test cancellation, reset, stale replies, Worker failure and restoration, with an explicit last-completed-result policy. Propagate real measured statistics consistently through the UI.
new: An anytime search could combine iterative deepening with cancellation and an explicit last-completed-result policy. Its telemetry should distinguish requested depth from completed depth and count work spent in aborted iterations. Tests should cover Reset, Undo, stale replies and Worker failure while confirming that interrupted search restores the input position.

text: 6. Evaluate user-facing behaviour. Run repeatable browser tests with real input, more viewport sizes and target devices; test the actual host integration separately. Measure end-to-end latency and frame timing in the intended environment, with enough repetitions and disclosed methodology. A human usability or difficulty study requires participants, protocol and consent before results can be claimed.

Measure end-to-end latency and frame timing in the intended environment, with enough repetitions and disclosed methodology. A human usability or difficulty study requires participants, protocol and consent before results can be claimed.
new: Application evaluation should extend to physical target devices and the intended host environment. Repeated measurements of response latency and frame timing would complement the present automated checks. A participant study could examine control usability and perceived difficulty, while a multi-seed tournament against stated opponents could assess playing strength. Both require a documented protocol before their results can support conclusions.

text: 7. Synchronize the educational presentation. Mark illustrative code and figures, link measured charts to their source data and update outdated labels. Ensure that a four-direction description corresponds to code that actually scans four directions, or labels a horizontal example accurately. Keep narrative claims distinct from executed results.

new: The teaching website should remain synchronized with the implementations it explains. Illustrative programs need explicit scope, especially where a horizontal example accompanies a four-direction rule description. Charts should link to the data and generation procedure that produced them. This would let readers move from an explanation to the corresponding source or experiment without confusing a demonstration with a measurement.
